summary: Proposed a mechanism for tagging the language of plain text using special Unicode characters. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 6082.

eli5.summary: This idea was to hide a little label inside a piece of text saying what language it is in. It was later retired.

questions: how can language be tagged in unicode text
what are unicode language tag characters
how do you mark language in unicode text
subtitle: A way to hide language labels inside Unicode text using invisible tag characters.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols sometimes need to mark which language a piece of text is in, but adding visible markup is cumbersome and interferes with the text content.
tldr.mechanism: Use special reserved characters from Unicode Plane 14 that are invisible and can only be used for tagging. Spell out language tags using these tag characters and embed them in the text before the text they apply to.
tldr.outcome: This mechanism never gained wide adoption and was made Historic status in favor of RFC 6082, which uses a simpler out-of-band approach via metadata instead of embedding tags in the text.

today: RFC 6082 replaced this approach as Historic, moving language identification outside the text to metadata instead of embedding it with invisible characters.

sections.title: The Problem of Language Tags in Plain Text
sections.content:
Plain text has no built-in way to say 'this sentence is French' or 'this word is Spanish.' Markup languages like HTML can do this with tags, but plain text protocols (like email or simple data formats) have no standard mechanism. Protocols like ACAP needed a lightweight way to mark language in UTF-8 text without using heavy markup syntax.

The challenge was to embed language tags in plain text in a way that is completely transparent to applications that do not understand tags—they should be able to ignore the tags and still process the text correctly.
sections.eli5: Some Internet protocols send plain text and need to say what language it is, but they don't have a good place to put that information.

sections.title: Plane 14 Tag Characters
sections.content:
Unicode is organized into 17 planes (large blocks of characters). Plane 14 is mostly reserved and was used for this proposal. The scheme defines 97 special characters in the range U+000E0000 to U+000E007F. Of these, 94 are tag versions of ASCII printable characters (like TAG A, TAG Z, TAG HYPHEN), plus SPACE and a few special control characters.

These tag characters look like their ASCII equivalents when displayed (if at all), but they can only exist in this special range and can only be used for tagging. Because they are in a completely separate range, code that processes text can easily identify and ignore them using a simple range check.
sections.eli5: Imagine every letter has an invisible twin. You use the invisible twins to spell out a language tag, and the twins are so special they can never be confused with real letters.

sections.title: Embedding and Scope of Tags
sections.content:
To tag a section of text as Japanese, the sender spells out 'ja' (or 'ja-JP') using tag characters prefixed by the LANGUAGE TAG character (U+000E0001). For example, the tag 'ja' becomes: TAG LANGUAGE + TAG j + TAG a. This sequence is simply placed in the text before the Japanese text it applies to.

A tag's scope continues until the text ends or until a CANCEL TAG character is encountered. Only tags of the same type can change the value (a new language tag replaces the old one). Tags of different types (if they existed) can nest or interdigitate. The RFC recommends lowercasing language tags before encoding them to tag characters for consistency with RFC 1766 practice.
sections.eli5: You put the invisible tag at the start of the French bit. Everything after that is French until you either end the text or put an invisible 'cancel' mark.

sections.title: Encoding Forms and Range Checking
sections.content:
The tag characters are defined in UCS-4 (the simplest form: U+000E0000 to U+000E007F), but need to work in UTF-16 (the two-unit form) and UTF-8 (the multi-byte form) as well. In UTF-16, tag characters are encoded as surrogate pair DB40 DC00 to DB40 DC7F. In UTF-8, they appear as sequences starting with F3 A0 80 and F3 A0 81.

Applications check if a character is a tag character using simple range checks appropriate to the encoding form they use. Because the ranges are carefully chosen, these checks can also be expressed as bitmask operations for efficiency.
sections.eli5: Tag characters can be written in different formats, and each format has an easy way to spot them.

sections.title: Unicode Conformance and Status
sections.content:
The tag characters were accepted for inclusion in the Unicode Standard and approved by the Unicode Consortium. However, they remain less widely used than hoped. Implementers were cautioned that until ISO JTC1/SC2/WG2 formally approved them, their use was experimental.

This RFC is now Historic status. RFC 6082 replaced it with a simpler, out-of-band approach where language information lives in metadata headers rather than embedded in the text itself. This proved simpler to implement and more robust in practice.
sections.eli5: This idea was approved by the Unicode people and became an official feature, but most programs never used it. A simpler way to mark language (using labels outside the text instead) became more popular.
